utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that we had a mechanical problem which delayed the start a little. It's yet to be proved to have been overcome, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with a preliminary matter before we call Ambassador Kypr. It was the topic that I mentioned on Tuesday evening in relation to the case for Sljivancanin, whether in actual fact the challenge was that Sljivancanin was at the JNA barracks and/or at Ovcara, and I think my learned friend reserved his position until this morning. I wonder, perhaps, if he could clarify that. It's clearly an important issue, because it goes to notice as well as other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to all. I had a look at the transcript. I must say, I had to go several times through that first portion referred to by Mr. Moore in order to understand what he meant. I hope that now I have a clearer understanding of the issue that he raised. First of all, as a matter of principle, I oppose such questions being asked by the OTP in the middle of the courtroom in the absence of the witness. This is entirely outside Rule 90(H). Allow me to clarify this. In keeping with my duties, I confronted the witness in no uncertain terms with the position of the Defence teams. The Chamber realised what the question was, the witness answered, the witness was examined on this issue on redirect. I think that we fully complied with all our obligations. After the witness had left the courtroom, Mr. Moore raised this issue requiring us to declare our position. Outside the context of this witness's testimony, I do not think the Defence is bound to share this sort of matter with the OTP at this stage of our proceedings. What the Defence could do about this was done at the pre-trial stage. I do not wish to leave my friend Mr. Moore entirely in the dark about this. Therefore, I will direct him to go back to the pre-trial brief for Mr. Sljivancanin, paragraph 118, and check that again. Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence made our position perfectly clear in relation to Mr. Sljivancanin's presence at the barracks, at the Velepromet meeting, since that appears to have been one of the issues raised in the OTP's pre-trial brief, as well as at Ovcara. I do not wish to waste any more time on this. I believe our position was made crystal clear in our pre-trial brief. The Chamber fully accepts and understands our position. There were no further instructions issued by the Chamber regarding these issues, and I believe we have complied with all our obligations vis-a-vis the Prosecution. This is, once again, paragraph 118 of the Defence pre-trial brief. Since we have already broached this subject, I would also recommend that they go to 120 and 121 of the pre-trial brief, of Veselin Sljivancanin's pre-trial brief. We made it perfectly clear in those paragraphs that the OTP's theory about Mr. Sljivancanin's presence at the barracks, the one that follows from their pre-trial brief, and Mr. Mrksic's alleged order being passed on to Mr. Sljivancanin for the transport to Ovcara referred to in paragraph 120 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief seems to be corroborated by the testimony of a certain witness; this is Witness 64. There is no need for me to say his name. Apparently he offered corroboration for this theory of the Prosecution. In our pre-trial brief, we clearly indicated that if you look at the summary of that witness's testimony, more specifically paragraph 9, at least the way the OTP seems to be interpreting that particular paragraph, that witness hasn't the foggiest idea that the buses ever left for Ovcara to begin with. Now the OTP wants us to clarify several matters, whereas their own theory at the pre-trial stage has remained unclear to say the least. This is a matter for further evidence, however, and we shall be saying more about it when the time comes. However, I do believe that firstly there is no obligation on our part to clarify this position to the OTP, since it is quite clear from our pre-trial brief. B, we are duty-bound to clearly familiarise the witness with all these matters and confront him with our theory and not to leave him in the dark about these details. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, would you please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this not -- this was raised not as an issue about compliance or non-compliance with rules, and it's not a matter which involves any consideration of whether it's appropriate that this be raised in the presence of the witness or not. I think you are seeing far more behind the question than is really intended. I'm putting myself, for a moment, in the position of Mr. Moore. He read the transcript of the questions and said, now, is it really that they are saying the major was not at the barracks and not at Ovcara at all; or are they saying the witness was wrong about certain things he said happened there. It was a point of clarification. What is in your original pre-trial brief may well provide an answer, I don't know, because I haven't looked back to it for this reason. But even if it's in your original pre-trial brief, as the trial proceeds it's quite possible that you change your position as more evidence becomes known, et cetera. So I think it's a fairly simple and uncomplicated and unsinister question that's being asked. Are you saying you were there or not. And Mr. Moore just asked, could you just make that clear. He might well have seen the confusion at the very end of the evidence and raised it then while the witness was here, but I think he was fairly frank in saying, look, when I go back and study the transcript, I'm not altogether clear, could it be clarified. I think you could say in half a dozen words whether your client was, in your case, at Ovcara or at the barracks or even at Velepromet, if you want to. Would you mind just helping us by saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I will do as you have ruled, which I fully respect. I just wanted to put forward my own position. I don't think this is the place or time to exchange this sort of comment between the parties. But the position of Mr. Sljivancanin, which is quite clear, based on the pre-trial brief, is that he was not at the barracks on the 20th at the time relevant to this indictment. His position is that he was not present at the Velepromet meeting. I believe the OTP have gathered as much since they have seem to have given up on a number of witnesses in relation to that and he was not at Ovcara. We were crystal clear about this in the paragraph that I quoted. I do agree with you that should evidence arise that might drive us to change our positions, we might want do so and we shall certainly clarify any further changes in our position to the Prosecution. But I believe our case is very often perfectly clear when we actually cross-examine witnesses. Much more so, in fact, that on some of the agreed facts. That is our position. We leave no witnesses in the dark and make our position perfectly clear to each and every one of then. Mr. Sljivancanin was at the hospital, that is part of the agreed facts now, but he was not at the barracks and not at Ovcara on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you happy with the note?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. We understand that your position is unchanged from the pre-trial brief. It is your case that your client was not at the barracks, not at Ovcara, and if it matters, for the moment, not at Velepromet at the times that are relevant. Now, Mr. Moore, that, I think, is what you sought?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you very much. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can have the witness, can we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Ambassador Kypr.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Before you get comfortable, could you please stand and take the card that's offered you and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Now Mr. Moore will be putting questions to you for a time. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: My full name is Petr Kypr.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you are of Czech nationality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That you are currently a diplomat?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that in actual fact you are an ambassador; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal just, please, with certain aspects of your background. I think it's -- is it right to say that you were employed as an analyst prior to 1990?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In what capacity was that? Apart from just analysing, what were you analysing specifically?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Frankly, from 1990 I was -- I passed the public competition to the foreign ministry. Then I was sent almost immediately after few days only, I was sent to the EC Monitoring Commission to the front line in former Croatia, and then I came back and I worked as analyst within the institute of international relations, which is a part of our ministry of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just try and break it up so that we understand? I think it's right it say that you were sent to the ECMM monitoring mission in Zagreb. I think that was in July 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I believe in December 1991 you returned to Prague and you were an analyst then, I think, for the ministry of foreign affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then in 1992 you were appointed ambassador in Slovenia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And your -- if I may the use the phrase, your tour of duty was from 1992 until 1997?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, from 1992 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's also correct to say that you speak seven languages?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And one of the reasons that you were sent there was because of your linguistic skills in the Balkans; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In 1997, is it also correct you were then appointed the director for the academy of the ministry of foreign affairs, I think you were responsible for setting it up?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, in very short terms or order, explain to us, please, what you had to do?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: You mean the academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. How you had to set up and what were the responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Because before I served in Slovenia as ambassador for almost five years, three years only alone with my wife, so I know almost all the diplomatic business, so I was probably the best person to establish a diplomatic academy which should prepare new diplomats for the new Czech diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to pause because while we are speaking in English, there has to be a translation. Then in 1998, is it right you were appointed the ambassador to Norway?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that appointment was until, I believe, 2003 [realtime transcript read in error "1993"]?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then 2003 I think it's right again that you were appointed --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the written translation. There is 1993, so it was 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, the question is 2003. Then in 2003 I think it's right that you returned?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you became head of the analytical department?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that was the ministry of foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And recently you have been appointed ambassador to another country, and I'm not going to mention that, as I think it has not been officially announced; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. May I just deal, then, please, with the period of 1991? I think it's right to say you told us that you went to Zagreb to the ECMM; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, the ECMM, so that everybody knows - and of course the Court do know - stands for the European Community Monitoring Mission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is a course that would meet the Court's approval, the ambassador falls into a slightly unusual category. As he was a monitor, there are a number of documents which I would seek to refer to in part or in whole, and perhaps seek to present them as exhibits. But he also has a witness statement where there is reference to the documents and they are in the context, I was going to make application that he have his statement in front of him so that there is the continuity in relation to the documents and his evidence. I don't know if that would meet with the Court's approval and my learned friends' approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we will see whether there is any obvious concern. It would seem to me to be help everybody to be able to follow documents in evidence. I see general concurrence on the faces of counsel. It has the concurrence of the Chamber, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are two copies for the witness. One is in English. May I pass that forward? And if he is really lucky, he can have the Czech copy as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But could we try and work in English, because the paragraphs are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, what I have had done, we have got a number of the documents in the electronic filing system in the court, but we also have prepared hard copies for the Chamber if they would wish to have that. And I've got them also for the Defence, if that would help. So I can hand those out, and we will of course call them up on to the electronic screen, produce them as we would, but sometimes hard copies are easier to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can they perhaps now be handed out, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ambassador, would you be kind enough, please, to turn up your statement?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right it say, if we just deal with bottom right-hand corner, I'm going to refer to the -- what's called the ERN number because of the records. If you look at the bottom right-hand corner I'll give you the last three numbers, which here are 685. Is it on your statement or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Excellent. Can we just deal with the first large paragraph. If I abbreviate it in the following way, I think it's right to say that there were a number of documents to which you had access, that you submitted them to the ICTY investigator Vladimir Dzuro, and some of those documents which you have submitted are copies of original ECMM documents which you completed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's also photocopied. May we deal then, please, with page 686? Again, linguistic remarks and abbreviations. We've also dealt with ECMM, which stands for European Community Monitoring Mission; ICRC, obviously International Committee of the Red Cross; MSF, Medecins sans Frontieres; and ICTY is obvious?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's right to say that for the understanding of the documents that you have compiled -- or it has been compiled a short glossary which can be found at divider, I hope, 2. So you have the documents, you were given a file. Would you be kind enough, please, to turn up divider 2?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, there are abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, it has the ERN number 1392?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm told perhaps it's prudent to call out all the numbers. The ERN number is 00381392, 00381393 in the English. I'm quite prepared to provide to the registry a copy of this index, which may assist in due course for accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, please, with the abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We can see first MD relates to 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And perhaps for the assistance of others many of the abbreviations are perfectly obvious. But LO is one that is used, liaison officer. And then we've got other matters which can be referred to in due course. And turning the page, 1393, again, we have got RDE, we stands for roles of engagement, or I suspect rules of engagement. And these are abbreviations which are used, as far as you are aware, throughout the documentation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But there were even other abbreviations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have little doubt of that, but we'll deal with those as we proceed.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moore, to establish a pattern, you've referred to this document, could it be tendered at this moment and dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I think probably the best course is to exhibit it as I go along. Otherwise what tends to happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Electronically it will be a nightmare if you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will tender the documents as I go along. It will be rather slow, but at least it will be efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. This will be received. That's tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we just turn over to tab 3 we can deal with this very briefly. I think it's right it say that this is a structure in relation to the way the ECMM was -- the hierarchy; would that be right or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we can see that your position is DHRCB?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What exactly does that stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It means that I was more or less advisor to the head of Belgrade centre. Belgrade centre means Belgrade centre of European Community Monitoring Mission, which was established in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to that, we can see that there are various teams that are referred to. Who was the head of the Belgrade mission?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: The head of the Belgrade mission was from, very beginning, Ambassador Perrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to deal with Mr. Cunningham. We have got CM?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we can see clearly that he's on the left-hand side. It's right to say, is it not, that Mr. Cunningham was a former army officer --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- of the Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think you operated with him on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in particular in Vukovar where I think he headed the monitoring mission at that time. And we'll deal with that in due course.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, Colonel Cunningham was a very experienced man from his previous military life. So the mission relies on them very much. It's why he was appointed as a chief of monitor, so he was responsible for the whole -- well, work of monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number there relates to ERN 00381390, 00381390, although I see it's 91, but I just wish to have the document of 90 before the Court as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please have clarified whether this was the organisation at a particular place or for the whole of the region of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have heard the learned Judge's question. This is clearly a structure. We will be hearing about Ilok and other villages and then Vukovar. When and where did this particular structure apply, can you tell us, if we deal with the time-scale August through to November?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: As I do remember, this structure was built in the beginning of September, when the regional centre was established in Belgrade, because until that time it was only in Zagreb. And then the mission recognised that it's necessary to have more places covered, so we established -- we, or European Community Monitoring Mission established centers in Belgrade and Sarajevo and in Split, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 303.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal, then, with a period when you went to Ilok. Now can we turn over to divider 4, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the document that I wish to refer to is L0053771, which is a translation. It's a final version of a draft concluding in 3772. Can we just look at the English version of that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not at tab 4, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have certainly -- I don't know if the Ambassador has. I have got it in B/C/S -- will Your Honour forgive me one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour have the document which says 34693?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: One is a draft and one is a final document. It should be a document dated the 16th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We certainly have 03034693. And I am asked, Mr. Moore, if you could be careful to give all the digits, because without all the digits the computer won't recognise just the last few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the other one we have at tab 4 is 00381350.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that you have referred to, or I have referred to, the 3771 was an original draft, and then it became a full translation, which should conclude in 03034693, and I think I am right in saying that the Court has got that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I said, we have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's the same. They've got two numbers, one is a draft and one is a final document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But we have only two documents in the tab. One of them is the original, and this is -- and the number you are dealing with is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to deal with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Which is 03034693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just to confirm for the assistance of counsel, it is tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got that document, Ambassador? Ilok urban community?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes. But I do have a draft translation in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll deal with that, in any event, because they are the same. Often we have draft and then final documents. Can we deal, please, with the document itself? Is it Ilok urban community?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is the date Ilok, the 16th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, in original copy that is the -- this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then I think it's the government of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there is a letter, "Dear Mr. Budisa"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, where this letter came from? If we look at the following page, we can see -- or on the same page, it's Anto ...

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: We got this letter, it means Belgrade's regional centre of ECMM. We got this letter through Zagreb. It was probably sent by fax or I don't know what is the source, but it is from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: From Zagreb. Exactly from our headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's -- it reads: "We take the liberty." May I move to the -- "We take the liberty of sending this letter to you in your capacity of a member, the cease-fire monitoring mission, in order to acquaint you with the situation in Ilok. Since we live in the most easterly part of the Republic of Croatia, which has been recently been encircled by the army, we believe there is a great danger of an army attack on the town." And the letter then goes on to refer to two serious incidents and then refers to the incidents themselves. Can we go to the bottom of the draft translation to help you? The reference is: "We intend to remain peaceful too, but we are prepared to defend ourselves to the last man if it should be necessary. We have negotiated with army representatives on several occasions, in our opinion with minimal results." And then finally: "A fortnight ago we evacuated the majority of the town's women and children to our coast and to Germany." Now, can we just deal with the Ilok matter. As a direct consequence of the situation at Ilok, not only from this letter but from other letters, is it right to say that the ECMM then visited Ilok?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes. We sent our teams many times. Practically immediately -- I remember that first team I was not a member of, was there sent the 11th or the 12th of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we then turn to tab 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for my part, I wasn't going to tender it. Merely refer to it for assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then move on to the next document, otherwise we'll have a large number of documents in the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But if we move to tab 5, and I will be seeking to tender this. Tab 5 is 0302 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Regarding the previous document, I also expected that my learned colleague would tender that into evidence, so I didn't initiate this question earlier, which needs to be clarified, and it's related to the witness's answers. If you look at the English translation of this previous document, 03034693, in the upper right-hand corner it states "VJ, Yugoslav army, 15th March 1996." In the original I don't see that text, so perhaps my learned friend could clarify that. Is there a mistake in the translation of this document perhaps, or it's something else, and the Defence has no way of knowing what it is. The witness already told us about the way in which he received this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, if you look at the original, are there not in the top right-hand quarter some handwritten markings? And are they not what is appearing on the translation in typed commencing with the word, "Handwritten."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence sees that there is something written in the upper right-hand corner but we are not able to read it. That's why I asked this question. It says "Vojska Jugoslavija," Yugoslav army. I don't see that there. It's possible that it is written there. That's why I wanted my learned friend to clarify whether this was a translation mistake or we were just not aware or informed about the markings in the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness may or may not be able to help, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think with regard to the handwritten, "Ky," if my memory serves me correctly, it's handwritten denoting the exhibits, so it would be "Ky" for Kypr and then with a stroke and then the number given. And indeed it is a feature you will find, I think, through all the exhibits that Ky -- so he is the producing witness, that is my understanding of the additional marks. But if that is not correct and my learned friend speaks to me at the adjournment, I will attempt to clarify, but that is my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The words "Yugoslav army," or "VJ," Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard Yugoslav army and VJ, I'm afraid I am not able to assist. I don't know if Ambassador Kypr will know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know, Ambassador where the phrase "Yugoslav army," where that --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, it is not in original text. And I agree that those written -- handwritten remarks are from my first witness statement only to mark those documents, so it has no sense to translate it as Yugoslav army, so I think that it can be easily deleted, because it is a mistake in translation, as I understand. But it's up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Ambassador, that these are your own handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. And you acknowledge that they don't help anybody about the content of the document? They're for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for my -- sorry, Your Honour. Not for my purposes. It was for a purpose for the first witness protocol or for witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist my learned friend is the way I'm trying to adduce the evidence is to marry up the witness statement which refers to the exhibit number Ky 1, or 2, or 11, with the documents and taking it in sequence. So that they were handwritten at the time for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. So if you go back to the index at the beginning of the folder, you see Ky-I-1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that is for purpose of preparing -- it's proofing notes, basically, Mr. Vasic. Does that help you? The mystery solved?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm grateful for that, Mr. Moore. Now, you're moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But can I remind you, please, to give all of the digits of the ERN number. Like me, you tend to drop out the zeros at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do. Does the Court require it in B/C/S as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the electronic system, yes. Any document you are tendering, whatever its language, the full ERN number is the only way that the court officer can find it. He doesn't have a folder, so he can't check it that way. He's got to have the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. May we move to tab 5? I'll give out the full ERN number, which might -- ERN 00381351, 00381351, that's in B/C/S. And then in English, 03029175, 03029175. I hope that that's right. It's got a handwritten Ky-I/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal with this document, please? I'd like to deal with the document in English, 03029175. We can see the date of the document, top left-hand corner, is the 16th of October?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That seems when it was actually transmitted. But the letter itself is dated, Vukovar, 13th of October, 1991. Have you got that there, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't know what is the source of this document. Sure we were now in the very centre of Vukovar in that time, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just please deal with the question? We can see if the Republic of Croatia, Municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Gives the details, gives class?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then we've got Vukovar, 13th of October, not November, 13th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is then directed to the various parties, we can see?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Various presidents. Subject is the mediation by the observers' mission from the area of the town of Ilok and the surrounding villages at request. And if we look at bottom right-hand corner, we can see that it is signed by Marin Vidic, Bili. You have that document in front of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just deal, then, please, with certain parts of the document. "[Initially] part of the municipality of Vukovar with the town of Ilok and the surrounding villages are mainly populated by Croatian inhabitants. So far, in the course of the armed clashes in the area of the municipality of Vukovar, the town of Ilok and surrounding villages have been spared from the conflict with the Yugo-army. As the Yugo-army suffered defeats in the western part of the municipality of Vukovar, it stepped up activities and, without any cause whatsoever, plunged into destructive activities in the eastern part, in the villages of Bapska, Sarengrad and Lovas." And there then is reference to the level of destruction and the population of 6.300 inhabitants in the town of Ilok growing to about 15.000. I won't go on to any other aspect of the document itself. Not because we don't accept it being true, but merely for time considerations. But as far as you are aware, is it right to say that at that time in and around the early part of October, there was concern within the ECMM to visit those villages and Ilok?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I tender that document as an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 304.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, may I move, then, please, to tab 6, which precedes it in time. Let me just read out the number. It is 00381353, 00381356. Then at 03033656, 03033658, and 03040101. And for the English 00366920, 00366920. Now, I think it's right to say that this is a document which is handwritten. Could we turn to divider 6, please, a handwritten document. I don't think you've got it there.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's team 7, and we've got the various names. Is -- are those people part of the ECMM monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we've got the names. And we've got mission Ilok. And we've got the 8th of October. May I just deal then, please, with certain parts of it, although I will seek to tender the document as a whole. There are the various details of timings in paragraph 1. Could you just stick on the -- this page, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then page 2, meeting with the authorities of Ilok --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- and with the JNA. And we've got what are called generalities. And if we look at subparagraph A3?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, actually subparagraph A2 is probably the starting point. The population of seven villages amount to, give or take, 15.000 people. And immediately above that there are the references to the villages in what could be called the Ilok area.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So Ilok, Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo, Opatovac, Lovac, and Tovarnik. And then subparagraph 3 there are the nationalities being described, or perhaps ethnicities. What was the percentage given, please, for Croats in this general area?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: There is written 65.7 per cent of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we turn over, then, please, and we'll deal with what's described as the current situation existing on the 8th of October. Would you be kind enough, please, to read out b, subparagraph 1?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: "All villages have been attacked by like JNA except Ilok and most of the population is now concentrated in Ilok and in difficult conditions."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we move on to paragraph 2, are you able to read it, or would you wish me to do it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I do have some problems because I passed an eye surgery last week -- last month, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, with the Court's leave, I will read it. "Ilok is completely surrounded by the JNA. Electricity, water and communications are cut off. For the time being, they have sufficient stocks of food, but the" -- I'm not sure what that word is, "supply from Backa Palanka and Sid is completely cut. There are shortages of medicines and baby food. There are four doctors in Ilok." May we move on to subsection (3). "Three months ago there were three mortar attacks by the JNA. Since then there have been several ultimatums asking them that the CNG should leave the villages and give back weapons. After these ultimatums, villages were attacked and shelled." I wonder if we could be kind enough, please, to turn up the large map that we use.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry to interrupt my learned friend, but what I would like to know is whether on page 25, line 18, when he quoted this paragraph 3, did he perhaps unintentionally omit -- "[In English] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is "minor" and, I think mortar was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies. Can we turn, then, please, to Exhibit 156?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, at the moment the court officer has a problem that may have moved from Judge Van Den Wyngaert's computer to his. A technician is coming. It means that at the moment he cannot open any of these exhibits. He can view them, we have them in paper, we can carry on, but he can't put them up on the screen at the moment. He also points out that at least with the last exhibit you tendered only the English and not also the B/C/S original. Did you want both?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I speak honestly and plainly for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You usually do, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I'm going to tender a document, and my learned -- I know that the registry have been fantastically helpful, but I think we have given them the index of the numbers. Surely it's not necessary to read out all the numbers. If I do one and, let us say it is the English version, it can be assumed, surely, that the B/C/S can be loaded into the computer without this rather strange system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It can be, but it must be clear on the record whether you tender both the English and the B/C/S, or merely the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just say then say that I will tender all documents, whether in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- and English from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, I think, can be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will carry on with paper at the moment. And we will have then, only one exhibit number for both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that's excellent. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Moore. As long as you can without it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to refer the Ambassador to Exhibit 103. That is the large group of maps. We have a copy for him, if he would be kind enough -- perhaps that could be passed to him, please. I believe this map can be shown on the screen, the electronic version, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not at the moment, because the earlier problem is being dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ah, on the ELMO, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ambassador, would you be kind enough, please, to look at this map? I'm hoping that it will show principally two colours. A yellow and an orangey-pink colour. Can we just look, please, at the yellow, which denotes Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And look at the been right-hand corner. We can see Ilok, Sarengrad, Lovas, and Bapska. Can you remember where the other villages that are mentioned on that document that you have in front of you, the 8th of October, the villages there are mentioned. You've got Ilok, Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo, do you know where --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It is in one of documents in tab number 6. There is a map which is -- which is, I think, more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. But we -- we have got a coloured version, and therefore if you can trans -- transmit --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Okay. So Opatovac and Mohovo are somewhere here. Tovarnik is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regard to the -- the mission that you had, or when I say "you" I mean plurally the ECMM, were you able to visit all the villages that were mentioned on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Not all of them each time. Sometimes we went only to Sarengrad, the other team was able to -- to go to other places. So it depend on the conditions and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's return to the handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have already referred to the ultimatums that, if we look at number 3, have you got that there? Left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Current -- "current situation." So it's tab 6, handwritten. I don't think it's that document. The one we were on. So we've got: "Current situation." Paragraph -- subparagraph 3, starting: "Three months ago." Where I had already mentioned 2.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Which is "minor."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, at the end of that paragraph: "After this ultimatums, villages were attacked and shelled." And there is reference to an ultimatum being given. And the document says: "See annex C." Now, I hope that, if one goes to the back of tab 6, we should be able to see a document which comes from the army to the people of Bapska. And the number, ERN number is 00366920. Would you be kind enough, Ambassador, please, to turn -- keep your hand on that handwritten page, and then go to the back of that tab? And it should read: "From the army to the people of Bapska."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal with Bapska? And I'll read it again to assist you. To the residents of Bapska. And from the army to the people of Bapska. "For some period of time now, JNA units stationed in the municipality of Vukovar" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to be interrupting all the time, but there's something that I would like to notice. In the original document, if that is indeed what the B/C/S version is, it does not say "from the army to the people of Bapska." It just says in the original document: "The local inhabitants of Bapska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps my learned friend can assist me, because the bottom right-hand part of the document says: "On behalf of the JNA," and then there's Major -- which the name is illegible. But in any event, if I read the document, and I'm sure it can be dealt with by cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "For some period of time now, JNA units stationed in the municipality of Vukovar have been subjected to attacks by the ZNG, MUP and armed civilians. "Since the residence [sic] of your village of Bapska were peaceful and did not cause any problems to JNA units, we assume that there will be no problems. We request the following: By 4.00 p.m. collect all the weapons in the village and bring it to Vikjaca where a body of the JNA will be waiting. Two, insofar as this is not done, your village will cease to exist on a geographical map. If you in any way hold up Tomic Borislav so that he does not return with your reply by 3.00 p.m. we will assume that you did not receive this ultimatum. Four, insofar as you do not wish to complete this ultimatum at 3.00 p.m. along with Tomic Borislav, inform us of this through your representative to whom we guarantee a safe return no matter of the success or failure of this ultimatum." And I have a date, the 28th of -- in the translation, the 28th of September, 1991. And it appears to be on behalf of the JNA, and then there is a major, and the signature is illegible. Is that right, Ambassador, or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And just for completeness sake, I can see that there is a fax particular up at the top, October the 15th, 1991. I don't know if it's on everyone's copy. And there is a reference to it. It seems to be in Zagreb. Now, do you know where this document has come from?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: This document was a part of the file of -- of the report of team 7, Simmons, Rodrigues, Martinez who went to Ilok and surroundings. It's all I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not going to refer to paragraphs 4 and 5. Can we deal with just paragraph 6? Again: "At present, the people of Ilok are living under a big stress. I think it's fearing that the JNA might attack in the coming days." Now, can we deal, then, please, turning the page, which is 1355, it's the same document. We can see top right-hand corner, three of seven. It's subsection C, and it is the visit of Sarengrad. Could you read out, please, what the findings were when they visited Sarengrad, where we have located that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: "We visited also the neighbouring village of Sarengrad, which was heavily damaged." I can't read it. Maybe in -- there is some transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it says actually: "The nuns of the convent have left for Ilok convent."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, then, please, with the miscellaneous items that were referred to in respect of the Ilok and the surrounding area? Can we deal with evacuation? Are you able to read what it says there, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes. "Some people would like to be evacuated as soon as possible. Others would rather be evacuated when an attack is imminent or had taken" -- I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Taken place?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: "Taken place."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I deal with 2 and 3, and I abbreviate, not trying to put any slant on it at all, just for completeness, there seems to have been that there was a meeting organised between the JNA and local authorities to discuss the situation, and after your visit at Ilok, you met -- the ECMM met the JNA colonel's secretary whose unnamed who gave assurance that the village wouldn't be attacked and at the moment they were trying to restore supply of water and electricity. However, can we deal then finally, please, with the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Conclusions, number 7a: "Arrangements at high level should be made to arrange an evacuation." And then in upper case letters: "As soon as possible." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then for continuity on the exhibits: "b, a team should be sent in two to three days to assess" -- presumably assess on the situation. "The team should get in touch both with the local authorities and with the JNA."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The following page there is reference to other visits to -- I see my learned friend is raising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- there is peace in the world. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And at page 1356 there is reference to an agreement with a JNA liaison officer. Your Honour, I'd seek to make the handwritten report, which I have referred to, then the map, which is in much more detail and refers to the actual locations that were visited as an exhibit. And also the -- what I will call the Bapska ultimatum in B/C/S and English, I seem them to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that the whole of the documents that are in tab 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not -- there are translations, and the only one that I was going to -- the ones that I was going to deal with were the -- the handwritten document, the Bapska ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then, you must give the poor court officer each ERN number that you are tendering page by page, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will. Well, then, the ERN number will be 00381353, 54, 55, 56, 1358, 1359 and 00366920. Those would be the only documents that I would seek to tender as an exhibit, unless my learned friends want some others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I seem to have jumped the gun a moment ago, but now I will give you the position of the Defence team. We are, for the time being, challenging the authenticity of this document, which I will call the same as Mr. Moore, an ultimatum to destroy the village of Bapska, dated the 28th of September 1991. We propose that it be given an identification number now. We have no objection to the other document that the Prosecution has tendered with the exception of this one. The explanation is this seems to be a handwritten document with no stamps or even any indication of whoever received this document. We will probably bring this up in cross-examination with this witness to see how exactly the witness submitted the document to the OTP and then we shall be expecting the OTP to confirm the authenticity of this document. We will be running our own checks, too. Based on the original document, there is a conversation with a colonel, there is reference there to a major, we don't know which one exactly. So for the time being, our position is where we cannot have this admitted without prior checks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the document is tendered as part of an ECMM report. The report itself is verified. Therefore, it is admissable as such. Now, your point, and an important one, is whether it can be relied on. Whether it is genuine or not. Now, that can be dealt with in cross-examination. And it may be that it will be shown to be not a true document or other evidence may confirm that it is what it purports to be. But in terms of admissibility, rather than the weight that can be attached to it, it is properly tendered as part of the present report. That leaves you entirely free to deal with the weight, if any, that should attach to it for our purposes later in the trial. Understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I do, Your Honour. Completely. I do have to make a comment, however. The Zagreb agreement, likewise, was a document submitted by the European Community Monitoring Mission. We challenged the document based on Mr. Raseta's signature. It was only marked for identification because of the misgivings surrounding its authenticity, and it is the same kind of verification that we would like to have now, although that document, too, was originally sourced from the European Community Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are testing my memory at the moment and, as always, it's likely to be different. But that, if I remember, was tendered separately and solely as a document, whereas this is tendered as report, and one of the parts of the report happens to be this document. Because the agreement was tendered entirely separately as a document, we were able for everybody's peace of mind to say, all right, we will hold that document at the moment until it can be looked at. Strictly we could have done with that what we are doing now with this report and this document. The end result is the same. You have clearly indicated you dispute the authenticity of the document so that it is an issue which has to be weighed. And in the end, whatever the evidence about the document and its authenticity turns out to be, the Chamber will have to evaluate that. So the end result, I think you will find, is the same. This group of documents will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first group of documents will receive the exhibit number 305, while the ultimatum will receive exhibit number 306.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we now move on to tab 7, because the last -- the last document was dated the 8th of October and referred to about a follow-up mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ambassador, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to tab 7?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just read out all the numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know interruptions are not helpful, but it is now that I understand nothing at all. It is now that the OTP is tendering the document as a follow-up. I thought it was supposed to be part of 306, that it would have been tendered as part of 306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The whole of the document, the report including the ultimatum, is one exhibit. I think the court officer is trying to be helpful. So it will all be the one exhibit, 305. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ambassador, would you be kind enough, as I say, to turn up tab 7.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We've got -- the date is the 12th of October, and I will be seeking to produce all these documents in B/C/S and English as exhibits. May I just refer to the ERN numbers at the very outset. 00381361, 62, 63, and 64. The translation of that is 03034006, 07, 08. And then there is reference to what has been called an agreement. The ERN number of that, I hope, will be L003498, L0043498. But there is a draft in being, which the Ambassador will have, and I will deal with that. But if I may just deal, please, with the original document, the first document, dated the 12th of October. We have got the names and nationalities. We have got your name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who else travelled with you, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It was Mr. Finakaliotis from Greece; and Waters, United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the task on the 12th of October?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: To visit Ilok and -- I can't read it. And speak about supply of water and electricity, number of refugees, food, medicine, supplies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's right to say that you went at 8.00 in the morning, came back at 7.00 at night?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there are other details that are mentioned. For example, meeting, I think, with the JNA. Can we deal, then, please, with the following page, top right-hand corner, we can see 2 of 3. It's says: "Report of RCB." Have you got that? It's a handwritten document?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It should start --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, "Report of RCB." I hardly can read it, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Team number 6?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we can see there there's the reference to the 12th of the 10th. The objective stroked out, but it is visit to Ilok. And then there is references to the contacts at that time, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is a name of the colonel. Can you read the name of the colonel, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Colonel Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then there is meeting of members of the Ilok community. There's references to their names, police authorities, Red Cross local representative and medical doctors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now can we deal with the paragraphs as they're numbered. So I want to deal with paragraph 1. I'll read, if it assists, and I hope I read correctly: "Situation (as reported to us) regarding Ilok is surrounded by the JNA who have gradually taken control of neighbouring villages." It appears to then read: "The non-Serbian population have concentrated in Ilok, (estimated 15.000). Water, electricity supplies are intermittent." It refers to low water pressure and food and especially medical supplies, or medicine supplies are becoming scarce. We were supplied by both sides with a copy of the ultimatum by the JNA made on the 11th of October to the people of Ilok. "The ultimatum," which is called an agreement in our annex, "was made under the authority of the JNA, and we were told by the Ilok community that the officer in charge of the military district ..." Can you tell us his name, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then there is reference at paragraph 3. I think it is: "Discussions with the town council revealed that they intend to have a referendum on the 13th of October about whether to evacuate the town in face of the threat from the JNA. Many people felt that evacuation was inevitable because they were surrounded by superior forces. We were specifically asked to make contact with the Croatian authorities in Zagreb." And then it goes on in the following page, top right-hand corner, 3 of 4. I think it is: "Make arrangements for a convoy of evacuees to proceed westwards with Croatia under Red Cross supervision along with EC monitors observing." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with 4: "We were told of minefields (laid by both sides) and of incidents in surrounding villages where Serbian nationalists," if that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "... have allegedly made attacks. We were told that 7.000 people have had medical treatment, and so medical supplies (normally obtained from the main hospitals in Vukovar or Novi Sad) are now unobtainable. The refugees were interviewed (many from the village of Lovas) who have been in Ilok for up to 20 days told us that they had lived peacefully with their Serbian neighbours (many have been in the district since 1945) but they have now felt they could not do so in the future." And I think it is right to say that it was the conclusion that there was no damage. "There has been no damage." What is the next word, are you able to say? "Noticed" --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Written --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Looks like the word "noticed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is "noticed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Noticed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "... by us in the town and we did not see any evidence of heavy weapons and only Territorial Defence men with light arms." Can I just deal with the -- we didn't see any evidence of heavy weapons, only Territorial Defence men with light arms. Are we referring to -- or who are we referring to? What group are we talking about when we are referring to light arms and no evidence of heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I believe that it is the report about the situation within city Ilok and it is the Territorial Defence of city Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then there is reference: "During our visit, there was a continuous sound of artillery fire, which the JNA colonel admitted came from the Vukovar direction." And then there is various suggestions which I wasn't going to go into, references to meetings and the involvement of the Red Cross. And then finally: "Further visits by monitors necessary, particularly on 14th of October." That is right, I think, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That was the report. Can we just deal, then, please, with, I hope, the number, it should refer to the agreement itself. Can you just turn over, please? I think that's it. You've got a draft version, unfortunately. Can we go to the very start of it.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope it should read: "Following the initiative of the inhabitants."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "The inhabitants to hand over the weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives held by citizens or paramilitary formations. The following agreement was reached at the meeting of the representatives of Ilok and the JNA held on the 11th of October." I will just deal with it, if I may, in the summary. Paragraph 1 there is reference to: "All local citizens and paramilitary organisations will hand all weapons, ammunition and MES regardless of the manner of the requisition to the military police unit. To safe entry" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Moore. Are you reading from a version that we don't have?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty that I have is actually as follows: I have got a draft version, as indeed the witness has. But there was an amended version, which the witness does not have but the Court has. I believe that in actual fact they should be very similar. Perhaps the way that we could deal with it is to give the witness this document which he hasn't got in his bundle and I can read it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: It is more helpful if he has the same as we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It certainly is; I have no doubts of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to note that they don't have the documents either and that they possibly could be placed on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, if we just -- it's the same document with a slightly different translation. Can we deal with 2, please.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "A safe entry to Ilok and searches of all private, public and state-owned buildings in Ilok as locations where weapons, ammunition and MES have been left, forgotten or hidden."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "... shall be made possible." Then 3: "Weapons, ammunition and MES." I see that there is a concern by my learned friend about something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My learned friend might be reading a trifle too fast. I am receiving interpretation, it is just still on the accurate side, if I may put it that way. But what my learned friend started quoting on line 41, lines 10 through 11. "[In English] ... state-owned buildings ..." [Interpretation] And the continuation is, I think it should be read out: "As a place where ammunition was left behind, abandoned or forgotten, as well as mines and explosives." My colleague has omitted to read out this portion, and I think it would only be fair to confront the witness with that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I can certainly read out the whole agreement, but I am trying to abbreviate as best I can. If my friend wants me to read out the whole agreement, then I will do so. But for the Prosecution purpose we only require really three or four points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are continuing to have a number of difficulties, Mr. Moore, with the process and the procedure. It's slowing us all down, and I think it's unsatisfactory from many view-points. We have reached the point where the tape will require that we adjourn now for 20 minutes. Can I suggest that first, with the court officer, you try and discuss a procedure that will enable him to bring the document -- identify it, and bring it up on the screen. That will enable the interpreters to follow it, because they are having a difficulty following your reading, especially because your reading is only part of documents, even parts of sentences and paragraphs. I know you are trying to focus on what matters to you, but in so doing you are of course producing a problem for the Defence. That might be discussed with counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will 20 minutes be adequate for us to improve the system, or shall we give you 25 or 30 minutes, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would have thought 20 minutes would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes, and hopefully we can come to a more satisfactory arrangement for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can make no promises, but my understanding is as follows: That the registry was given a list of documents that we were calling. We have always presented them in the way that a tab, if I may use that, a tab number would refer to an exhibit. And that exhibit, therefore, would perhaps contain three or four documents. And I think that was a misunderstanding, perhaps, between my learned friend Ms. D'Angelo and the registry. Perhaps the best way of dealing with it is as follows: I understand my learned friends would like for their clients the B/C/S version to be put on the electronic screen so they can follow it. The difficulty we have, and I think it's just with e-court generally, is that if I put the B/C/S version on the screen, then the interpreters cannot see the English version, because you cannot do it simultaneously, and therein lies the difficulty. And I also believe that e-court was not working for some of the screens this morning for about 50 per cent of the time. So I, for my part, will call out the numbers for the B/C/S, and I will try and go slowly for the interpreters. The difficulty is that I try and use part of a document rather than all of a document, to focus on the points that I believe are important, and I will try and deal with it as tightly as I can if there are paragraphs numbered. The other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say, interrupting you, just so that the point is not lost. Quite obviously it's a waste of everybody's time if you read the whole of every document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you want to emphasise particular parts, you should at least try to read a full sentence, a full paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- rather than a part of it, so that the sense of that part is conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If then other parts of the document are seen by Defence counsel to be important, they can be referred to in cross-examination. What is potentially dangerous is for you to read only part of a sentence and leave the balance, which may have a different emphasis, unsaid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that, I think, will go a long way to helping Mr. Vasic. And it will probably help the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I make one further suggestion? Ms. D'Angelo has got her own brilliant system for putting the ERN numbers and the translations, because one of the problems that we have encountered is that often with translated documents they can have three or four numbers, and you can have, quite literally, I'm looking at one, where there are five groups of numbers which are needed for the electronic screen. I wonder if it might be prudent, if the numbers are to be referred to, if Ms. D'Angelo would be permitted to call out the numbers that apply. I know that she's spoken to the registry about that. Because I think there is a level of uncertainty about the actual index itself and the understanding from the registry's perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that will help convey what's in your minds to the registry, I think it will be a good idea. Now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're still warming up, what is important is that our clients understand the witness's testimony. One thing I asked the OTP during the break, they have provided a copy each for the Defence teams. Can these binders please be provided for our clients too, especially when we come to documents relating directly to Vukovar? It will be important for our clients to follow closely. I don't think it should be a problem to provide these during the next break, because we are now sharing with our clients our own binders. It is essential for each of the accused to follow the proceedings closely, just as it is for us in order to conduct our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't know at all whether that will be practical and feasible for that to be done. That's a matter which can be sorted out between counsel. But Mr. Moore will now be calling out the B/C/S numbers and they should appear on the screen, which will enable your clients to see the documents as we go. That is the correct understanding, is it, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps we can get along with the evidence, as the poor ambassador who has been waiting patiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will deal with the agreement. In English the number that I have for that is 00583520, and the B/C/S number is 00381364. If that, perhaps, could be put on the screen to assist the defendants. Now, I've got it on my screen, but it's very bad. The focus -- there is no focus at all. Could my learned friends please clarify whether their defendants can see the document or not? It seems that they can.
